abstract: Stripe Economics analysis examining where new businesses are forming on the Stripe platform and whether AI is loosening the tie between entrepreneurship and dense urban centers. The piece documents a continuing dispersion of business formation away from large metros and away from city centers within metros, while noting that the AI frontier itself remains extraordinarily concentrated. Close to 40% of new businesses on Stripe this year are in metros with fewer than one million people, up 10% relative to four years ago. The small-metro shift shows up at the extremes: Cheyenne, Wyoming now forms roughly twice as many businesses per person as New York City, against rough parity in 2022. Within metros, the movement is toward the edge — close to 80% of sign-ups in major metropolitan areas are outside the city center and the high-density inner ring, and in Houston 37% of new businesses are forming in the outer suburbs this year, up four percentage points relative to 2023. The authors size the overall shift as roughly one third as large as the COVID-era move away from major cities, so it is real but smaller than the pandemic reallocation. The counterweight is concentration at the frontier: almost 80% of AI businesses closest to the technological frontier — the labs — are in San Francisco alone. The authors are explicit that AI cannot be cleanly disentangled from remote work as the driver, though they note formation appears uncorrelated with work-from-home intensity.
keyFindings: Close to 40% of new businesses on Stripe this year are in metros with fewer than one million people, up 10% relative to four years ago — a continuing shift of formation toward smaller metros.
Cheyenne, Wyoming now forms roughly twice as many businesses per person as New York City; the two were at rough parity in 2022.

Within major metros the movement is outward: close to 80% of sign-ups are outside the city center and high-density inner ring. In Houston, 37% of new businesses are forming in the outer suburbs this year, up four percentage points relative to 2023.
The overall geographic shift is roughly one third as large as the COVID-era move away from major cities — directionally consistent but substantially smaller than the pandemic reallocation.

The AI frontier runs the opposite direction: almost 80% of AI businesses closest to the technological frontier (the labs) are in San Francisco alone. Dispersion in general business formation coexists with extreme concentration in frontier AI.
methodology: Descriptive analysis of new business sign-ups on the Stripe platform, aggregated by metro area and by within-metro density ring (city center, high-density inner ring, outer suburbs), compared across years. Metro-level formation is normalized per capita for cross-city comparisons. The COVID-era reallocation is used as a benchmark to size the current shift. Frontier AI concentration is measured as the share of AI businesses at the technological frontier by headquarters location.
qualifiers: Tier 2. Published on a Substack (stripeeconomics.com) rather than peer-reviewed. The underlying data are proprietary Stripe platform sign-ups, which cannot be independently replicated and are not a representative sample of US business formation — Stripe skews toward online-first and payments-enabled businesses, so the geographic pattern may partly reflect who adopts Stripe rather than who starts a business. The authors state explicitly that AI cannot be cleanly disentangled from remote work as the cause, though they note formation appears uncorrelated with work-from-home intensity. The classification of businesses as AI or frontier-AI is the authors' own and is not defined in detail. Descriptive correlations only; no causal identification.
